newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Top U.S. general discusses N.Korean threat in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. general discusses N.Korean threat in Seoul.

text.p: The chairman of the U.S. military Joint Chiefs of Staff met his South Korean counterpart on Tuesday to discuss the threat from North Korea as it grapples with a food crisis, a Seoul military official said.
John Shalikashvili arrived in South Korea earlier on Tuesday for a two-day visit, which will overlap with a trip to Seoul by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen.

Shalikashvili and Yoon Yong-nam discussed security on the Korean peninsula and steps to hone readiness against any attack from North Korea, said a spokesman for the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea to defend against the communist North.

Shalikashvili and Yoon "agreed North Korea was in a state of crisis due to a severe food shortage and pledged their two countries would cooperate to defend against any emergency situation on the peninsula", the spokesman said.
International relief agencies say North Korea is just weeks away from mass starvation following two consecutive years of devastating floods.

North Korea has told international aid agencies in Pyongyang a total of 134 children have died of malnutrition so far in the country's growing food crisis, a United Nations official said in Geneva on Tuesday.

Hans Olsen of the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF said the figure -- believed to be the first on mortality from food shortages provided by the secretive communist state -- was given by a health ministry official at a meeting on Monday.
There are constant fears in South Korea that the impoverished North may be tempted to play its final Cold War card against the South and lash out in desperation using its million-strong army.
U.S. officials insist they have no evidence of unusual military movements in North Korea.
On the contrary, there are signs that Pyongyang may be about to accept a proposal for four-way peace talks involving the two Koreas, the United States and China.
The spokesman said Shalikashvili made no mention of a controversy over Russian efforts to sell SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles to South Korea.
Cohen, who arrives on Wednesday, urged on Saturday South Korea not to buy the Russian missiles, suggesting they might accidentally threaten friendly U.S. jets in the confusion of any new Korean war.
Cohen said it would be a political and military mistake for U.S. ally Seoul to accept Russia's offer instead of buying American Patriot air defense missiles.
